description:
This video ends up more as a discussion of the GPU market right now, and in particular, the NVIDIA Super series lineup for RTX 40. The NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 Super gets reviewed here and benchmarked vs the AMD RX 7900 XTX, NVIDIA RTX 4080, and we also compare the entire NVIDIA lineup (including the RTX 4090, RTX 4070 Ti Super, RTX 4070 Ti, RTX 4070 Super, RTX 4070, RTX 4060 Ti, and RTX 4060). There are a lot of cards to discuss right now and this piece will kind of re-center everything after weeks of reviews.

If you want the most recent review data in raw format, you can check out these two videos:

RTX 4070 Ti Super review: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QruyaA0ZrLk

comments.text:
Looking at it 6mo later. It does seem the main move for releasing it as a new product was to mitigate the "First Review Stigma" that the 4080 had.

The majority of consumers look at the first reviews of a product before buying it, not review updates. 

So, the large (relative) value increase of the 4080 Super with the price drop with it having similar/slightly better performance versus the 4080 would sort of be lost in the noise over the reviews of the OG 4080 if they just rather dropped the OG 4080 by 200$. 

So, releasing a new product would "reset" reviews there, which is probably why they did it as people would see the new price and review from the POV of that price, and therefore value propositions would be reset for consumers looking at those 4080 Super Reviews. 

As for the actual value of the card, at it's current value unless you need the VRAM, it's pretty great. While it is annoying that the SKU is up a stack level. It at least is back to sort of where it was in the universe assuming Ampere cards sold at MSRP (or the Turing gen).

The names are different. But a buyer of an RTX 3080Ti would get a similar increase to performance going to the 4080 Super as they would be if they came from a RTX 2080Ti before owning their 3080Ti (while being a bit better value as the 4080 Super is lower MSRP than both)

Is it kinda sucky that the SKU names and prices have drifted? sure. But performance for the Lovelace Stack beyond the RTX 4060 family is kinda back to the Ampere-Generation MSRP levels for the most part.

- RTX 4070 is now within inflation rate cost of the 3070's MSRP and brings 3080+-level performance which is good gen-on-gen.
- 4070 Super is the price of a 3070Ti but beats the 3090 which is a very good value proposition gen-on-gen.
- 4070 Ti Super does have value drift a bit versus the 3080, being 100$ more and giving an on-average 30% increase gen-on-gen (and can vary a lot more).
- 4080 Super is 200$ cheaper than the 3080Ti was, but gives a 40% performance increase on average from what I can tell (So major value increase)

Then the 4090 just kind of exists at the high end but being a super value 3090Ti (relative) due to while the 4080s have a big perf increase over the 3080Ti/3090. The gap to the 4090 is even more gargantuan which probably is part of the source reason for the product performance stack versus names/prices being so funky.

comments.text: Thumbs down for Gamer's Nexus from publishing a FPS/dollars chart. You guys should know better. FPS/dollars are objectively meaningless (they would be meaningful only if you could linearly add as many GPUs into your system as you pleased, like bytes of storage, but as you know, you can only have one GPU for games tasks nowadays). Anyone who says otherwise unfortunately don't understand the mathematics. FPS/dollars mislead the viewer into thinking they are seeing statistics, but instead they are given garbage. Instead, please be respectable journalists and publish Pareto frontier charts of FPS on X-axis and dollars on Y-axis and plot the frontier on that. Such charts showcase the correct information that people looking at FPS/dollars don't understand they instead are looking for, without any incorrect maths. And as added bonus, Pareto charts distinguish between the objective and subjective clearly to the reader, instead of playing into any flamebait fanboy wars. Gamer's Nexus, please never publicize another FPS/dollars chart again, but keep your standards high, and present the correct Pareto frontier charts instead. Thanks!

comments.text:
Hey Steve...just an interesting one for you to consider when thinking about GPU prices in reviews...yes they're high and they seem whacky...however, if you inflation adjust the launch prices of the 1070, 2070 and 3070 and compare to the price of the 4070...you'll see that the 4070 price is below inflation...the 4080 is somewhere around 5-10% above inflation, depending on the board...pricing hasn't settled on that yet, so it's hard to work out...so right now, the 4070 price is actually pretty reasonable...relatively speaking...but the 4080 price is higher than it should be.

I know there are many other factors at play that determine the price of a card and whether the price reflects value...but it's one to consider...it's a much more useful and a lot less abstract than "cost per frame"...cost per frame is only useful for comparing one card to other cards, it is not useful for putting the price increases into perspective...using inflationary adjustments puts the prices into perspective and shows you how expensive the card actually is compared to previous generations and is less boring than "number go up, GRRRRR!".

comments.text:
Steve, I know you are hesitant to use the $/frame means of measuring value for a GPU, but there ARE people that exist that only cares about that - i.e. me.  I have a set budget, and I want to know which card can give me the best bang for buck, and I usually disregard extra bells and whistles provided by both companies because all they do is obfuscate things for me.  In other words, I kinda approach it like the old days when we mainly had cards that didn't contain these extra features because of the variability of said features, not all software supports RT.  I don't play mainstream Western games that require these extra features,.

I already have certain parameters in mind when I'm trying to buy a card.  1440p/120hz gaming, or perhaps 1440p/60hz minimum gaming on the highest settings and take it from there.

That's why your charts that display every type of scenario, 1080p gaming with/without RT all the way up to 4k gaming is useful, because we're able to take the data that is in those charts and apply it to the cards we're looking at buying.  We can even calculate our own $/fps for our specific scenario.  So don't think that you're catering to a small crowd or that you feel the data isn't useful - it is.  The GPU market is a mess and we're forced to perform all these tests JUST to get the info we need to buy the card we want to minimize how much it hurts to buy these cards.

I don't like cost per frame because:
- people don't buy only a GPU, to use by itself in ideal performance conditions. The impact of price differences goes away if you consider the cost of, say, a whole PC. Similarly, if that gpu is going into a system with a 4 year old i5, the impact of the performance differences also lessen. 
- it ignores frame pacing and features (the former mitigatable by using a transformation of the fps value like a multiplier based on the variance of the frame times)
- it ignores "the impact of higher fps games being greater than lower fps games in the avg" (mitigatable by normalizing fps before averaging)

Sadly as you may notice I don't have an answer for the first issue, because, well, everyone's situation is different

As I see it, in the past the point was you either buy one top of the line GPU (like xx80Ti) or for roughly the same or less money you could buy two medium-level GPUs like xx60 series. You'd get same or better performance for sligtly more heat and power consumption. But then it degraded in steps: 
-- on 1000 series you could just do SLIand run up to 4 GPUs
-- on 2000 series you needed an expensive NvLink bridge and could join only 2 cards
-- on 3000 series you still needed an NvLink bridge, but only the most expensive and power-hungry cards had the NvLink connector
-- on 4000 series none of the cards have a connector for NvLink, and I expect driver support to be dropped relatively soon as well

What part of video editing do you find VRAM makes a difference to? I've worked in film and video editing and post-production for over two decades, on a lot of different systems, and while more VRAM can improve responsiveness in compositing applications, I notice almost no difference during actual video editing. The files are simply too big to fit in VRAM, so that tends to be limited either by storage speed or processing speed (meaning CPU speed or GPU speed, depending on what is doing the processing).

Is there something specific about your editing pipeline (or maybe some specific plug-in?) that uses a lot of VRAM?

comments.author: @user9267

comments.text:
@user9267  - Not only can they work with proxies (that has been done for over 30 years), nearly all modern video editing (and compositing) software will automatically switch to a lower resolution for real-time previews, if they can't keep up.

The preview window is generally less than 1/4 of the screen anyway, so you don't even need the full resolution while you're editing.

And even at full resolution, VRAM has a very small impact, unless you're doing 3D effects with a lot of very large textures (that do need to be loaded in to VRAM, at least if you want to use GPU acceleration).

Video files are typically hundreds of gigabytes, there's no way you're going to fit them in VRAM (even if there was any point in doing so, and in most cases there isn't). They're just streamed off the drive(s), each frame (or GOP) is decompressed, effects are applied, and the result is saved to a new file (or just shown on the screen in real time, and then discarded).

If you're doing 4k+ compositing with massive textures and GPU-accelerated plug-ins (or if you want to preview long clips in real time at full resolution, uncompressed), sure, you need more VRAM (and more system RAM as well). But no one calls that "video editing". That's compositing (or just "effects"). And nothing in GN's videos suggests they're doing complex compositing.

comments.text:
@masterluckyluke  Performance uplift vs last gen doesn't mean it's that class of a card.

The 780 had a 384 bit memory bus.

The x80 class cards since then were downgraded to 256.  It was the Ti's that were all 384 instead (or 354).

The only exception to this has been the 3080 (320 bit), which was held back in other areas (less VRAM than the 1080 Ti is atrocious).  On paper the 3080 was about double the performance of a 1080 Ti, but in reality at higher resolutions it capped more around 75%.  I returned mine because the performance uplift wasn't as expected.

The 4080, and 4080 Super, both have lower memory bandwidth than the 3080, because NVIDIA downgraded back to 256 bit.  If both GPUs had the same core, the 3080 would be faster, especially at higher resolutions.

This is why I, and many others, say the modern GPUs (of both MFGs now) are a class below their naming scheme.

The 4090, sadly, is the only "real" GPU released in the last 5 years, and should've been named a 4080 Ti regardless.  The 3080 was great if you didn't have a 1080 Ti though; another small "mistake" NVIDIA won't make again.

comments.text:
@DeadNoob451  Efficiency literally increases the value, because it reduces total cost of ownership. Doing some of the math, as someone who works in game engines throughout the work-day, my PC rarely dropping to low power states. A conservative saving of 100W for ~8 hour a day, at 95% PSU efficiency, at local energy prices, saves about $120 a year. If I keep the card for 3 years, that's a $360 saving over those years. That's solely considering work time.

There are tons of additional factors too, if it's winter, that power usages actually heats the room (which is desirable), but if it's summer, you might end up with an uncomfortably warm room, or have to run an AC which is extra costs. There's also noise from fans, more power requires more cooling, which makes more noise, or adds more cost to get better cooling. Overall, efficiency is a very important, often overlooked factor.

The notable differences though is that the memory bus width on the 3080/3080ti is significantly larger than the 4080/4080 super even though they have more memory. For example it's 384bit on the 3080 ti and 256bit with the 4080 super. Really disappointing that Nvidia keeps nerfing their cards with small memory bus width.

comments.text: ​ @username8644  The bus width drop isn't a deliberate nerf. It's just the math required to achieve different capacities with different DRAM densities. Going from 12x1GB dies on the 3080Ti to 8x2GB dies on the 4080S with 32 signals lines to each just does that, and the 4080S has higher clock speed DRAM and 64Mb L2 cache while the 3080TI has 6mb with higher latency. There's only so much real estate on a card you can put DRAM chips on that's close enough to the die to maintain signal integrity, you can't just throw an ever-growing number of DRAM dies on a card with increased pinouts on the GPU die to keep the bus width climbing.

I upgraded from an I7-4770k w/ Asus gtx 1080 to an I7-13700k w/ Sapphire 7900xtx in late 2023. 

My honest review: disappointing. The performance is a significant boost over my old Haswell cpu, especially felt over zip/unzipping files and video editing. Gaming is great but not noticeable unless you are using a 4k monitor. I only use a wide-screen 2k 144hz monitor. 

Because Intel moved their IVR (integrated voltage regulator) to the motherboard instead of having it on the cpu (like Haswell), the responsiveness feels sluggish. Basic pc usage feels slow compared my old 4770k. It definitely feels like a downgrade. Not to mention its heat generating wattage usage.....

Because I "was" in your similar current pc set up, I would suggest you to just wait. It's really not worth upgrading yet unless you decided to go the AMD ryzen route.
